title: Hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis
subject: gastroenterology
setting: Emergency department, ward, HDU, ICU, clinic
summary: Grade with West Haven, protect the airway in grade 3 to 4, search for and treat precipitants (infection, bleeding, constipation, electrolytes, sedatives), give lactulose to 2 to 3 soft stools a day with early rifaximin, and continue secondary prophylaxis after the first episode.

sections.title: Recognise and grade
items: Suspect in any patient with cirrhosis, TIPS or a portosystemic shunt who has confusion, disorientation, sleep reversal, personality change, somnolence or coma. HE is a diagnosis of exclusion.

West Haven grade 1: subtle inattention, euphoria or anxiety, impaired calculation (covert). Grade 2: lethargy, disorientation to time, inappropriate behaviour, asterixis. Grade 3: somnolent to semi-stuporous but rousable, gross disorientation. Grade 4: coma.
Overt HE is grade 2 or higher. Asterixis alone, without cognitive or behavioural change, is not enough to diagnose overt HE.
Use the Glasgow Coma Scale alongside West Haven when consciousness is impaired.
Serum ammonia is not needed to diagnose HE or guide treatment. A normal ammonia in a confused patient should prompt a search for another cause.

sections.title: Airway, glucose and triage
items: Grade 3 to 4 or falling GCS: admit to HDU or ICU; intubate if the airway cannot be protected (aspiration risk).
Check capillary glucose immediately and treat hypoglycaemia (below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L)).
Alcohol use or malnutrition: give IV thiamine before glucose-containing fluids to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
Nurse head-up with aspiration precautions. Place a nasogastric tube for lactulose if the patient cannot swallow safely.
No routine brain imaging unless there are new focal neurological signs, head injury, seizures or another reason to suspect a structural cause.

sections.title: Find the precipitant
items: Infection: blood and urine cultures, diagnostic paracentesis if ascites is present (SBP), chest X-ray.
GI bleeding (melaena, falling Hb), constipation, dehydration or diuretic excess, AKI, hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia.
Drugs: benzodiazepines, opioids, gabapentin or pregabalin, sleep medicines (zolpidem), alcohol. Review and stop where possible.
Consider other causes of altered mentation: intracranial bleed, stroke, drug overdose, meningitis, Wernicke encephalopathy, hypercapnia, sepsis-associated encephalopathy.

sections.title: Treat overt HE
items: Treat each precipitant: antibiotics for proven or strongly suspected infection (no empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics without evidence of infection), correct electrolytes and volume, stop sedatives, hold diuretics if volume depleted.
Lactulose 10 to 20 g (15 to 30 mL) orally or by NG tube every 2 hours until 2 soft bowel movements, then 2 to 4 times daily titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools a day.

Cannot take oral or NG lactulose and anal tone preserved: lactulose enema (300 mL lactulose solution in 700 mL water or saline, retained 30 to 60 minutes, every 4 to 6 hours until mental state improves).
Add rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily to lactulose in hospitalised overt HE (ACG 2026). Its added value is small in ICU patients already on broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Polyethylene glycol (4 L) is an alternative cathartic, useful if lactulose causes distension or ileus.
Expect improvement within 24 to 48 hours. No recovery after 48 to 72 hours of adequate therapy: re-look for missed precipitants, other diagnoses or a large portosystemic shunt.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: West Haven grade or GCS at least daily (more often in grade 3 to 4), stool frequency and consistency, fluid balance.
Sodium, potassium and creatinine daily: over-purging with lactulose causes dehydration, hypernatraemia, hypokalaemia and AKI, which worsen HE.
Intubated patients with a faecal management system: hold lactulose if stool output exceeds 300 mL/day.

sections.title: Prevent recurrence
items: After a first episode of overt HE: lactulose titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools daily long term (strong recommendation, ACG 2026).
Recurrence despite lactulose: add rifaximin 550 mg twice daily (strong recommendation).

Protein 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day (up to 2 g/kg/day if critically ill); do not restrict protein. Late-evening snack; branched-chain amino acids if protein needs are not met by food. Consider zinc if serum zinc is low and HE persists.
Advise no driving after overt HE in the past 3 months; educate caregivers; review sedatives and unnecessary PPIs at discharge.
Refer for liver transplant assessment. Start rifaximin 14 days before elective TIPS and continue for at least 6 months. Refractory HE with a large shunt: consider shunt embolisation.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Relying on blood ammonia to diagnose or titrate treatment.
Protein restriction, which worsens sarcopenia without shortening HE.
Missing SBP or GI bleeding as the precipitant.
Excess lactulose causing dehydration and hypernatraemia; sedating an agitated patient with benzodiazepines.

drugs.name: Lactulose (oral or NG)
drugs.dose: 10 to 20 g (15 to 30 mL) every 2 hours until 2 soft stools, then 2 to 4 times daily to 2 to 3 soft stools a day
drugs.notes: Same target for long-term secondary prophylaxis. Titrate with stool frequency and Bristol stool scale.

drugs.name: Lactulose enema
drugs.dose: 300 mL lactulose solution in 700 mL water or 0.9% saline, retained 30 to 60 minutes, every 4 to 6 hours
drugs.notes: When oral or NG route is unsafe; needs preserved anal tone.

drugs.name: Rifaximin
drugs.notes: Add to lactulose in acute overt HE and for recurrence despite lactulose; start 14 days before elective TIPS.

drugs.name: Polyethylene glycol 3350-electrolyte solution
drugs.dose: 4 L orally or via nasogastric tube
drugs.notes: Alternative cathartic to lactulose (ACG 2026 conditional recommendation).

drugs.name: Thiamine
drugs.notes: Alcohol use or malnutrition. Use higher treatment doses if Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected.
